transcript.content: Hello, I am Dr. Smith. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Dr. Smith. I'm here because I've been struggling with episodes where I eat extremely large amounts of food. During these times, I feel a complete loss of control, like I just can't stop myself.
After these episodes of overeating, do you engage in any behaviors to prevent weight gain, such as self-induced vomiting, excessive exercise, or the misuse of laxatives?
No, I don't do anything like that. I have never forced myself to throw up, used laxatives, or tried to exercise excessively after an episode.
During or after these episodes, do you often experience feelings of being uncomfortably full, eating much more rapidly than normal, or feeling disgusted, depressed, or very guilty about your eating?

I definitely eat much faster than normal during these episodes, almost like I'm in a rush. However, I don't really experience feeling uncomfortably full, or feeling disgusted, depressed, or guilty afterward.
To better understand the pattern, how many times per week on average do these episodes of rapid eating and loss of control occur, and for how long has this been happening?
These episodes happen at least once a week on average. I have been struggling with this pattern for about two years and one month now.
During these episodes, do you find yourself eating an amount of food that is definitely larger than what most people would eat in a similar period of time under similar circumstances?

Yes, absolutely. I definitely eat a much larger amount of food during these episodes than what most people would eat in a similar situation. It is way more than what anyone would consider a normal portion or meal.
Do these episodes typically occur in secret or when you are alone because you feel embarrassed about how much you are eating?
Yes, I almost always do this when I am completely alone. I feel so embarrassed about the huge amount of food I'm consuming that I make sure no one else is around to see it.

Although the patient denied feelings of guilt, disgust, or depression (which are associated features rather than mandatory diagnostic criteria), the other clinical features are highly consistent with the diagnosis. No other candidates are currently suspected.
